title: The Pajama Factory Experiment
text:
At the Harwood pajama factory in Virginia, managers often had to change how jobs were done as styles and methods changed. Each time, output dropped, complaints rose and many workers quit. The personnel manager Lester Coch and the psychologist John French decided to test whether the way a change was introduced made a difference.

When the next set of small job changes came, they handled groups of workers in different ways. One group was simply told what the new method and piece rate would be, as usual. Another group chose representatives who helped study the job and design the new method. In two further groups, every worker took part in the discussion and planning.

The group that was simply told showed the familiar pattern: output fell and stayed low, there was open hostility toward management, and several workers left within weeks. The groups that took part recovered quickly and soon exceeded their old output, with the fully involved groups doing best. Later, the members of the first group were moved to another new job, this time with full participation, and they too recovered quickly.
lesson: Resistance to change is often a reaction to being left out. Involve the people affected in shaping the change, and they will help make it work.
location: Harwood Manufacturing Corporation, Marion, Virginia, USA
source: Coch, L., and French, J. R. P. (1948). Overcoming resistance to change. Human Relations, 1(4), 512-532.
